title: How to Become the Colleague Everyone Wants on Their Team
author: Ron Friedman
summary: In a guest post on Ethan Evans' Level Up newsletter, social psychologist Ron Friedman distills findings from his survey of more than 6,000 knowledge workers about what actually makes someone a valued teammate. Contrary to popular assumption, traits like being caring, a good listener, or funny ranked lowest in what colleagues said mattered most; the traits that rose to the top all had a direct, measurable effect on team performance. Friedman identifies several concrete behaviors that separate what he calls Superteams from average ones: actively elevating colleagues' work, sharing credit rather than absorbing it, embedding everyday appreciation rather than leaving it to managers, and deliberately shrinking status differences so everyone feels equally able to contribute. One of his most striking findings involves a simple hypothetical -- what workers say they'd do with unexpected free time -- where Superteam members defaulted to helping a colleague far more often than average-team workers. The piece is framed as practical career advice: since reputation increasingly rests on how colleagues experience working with you, these specific behaviors are levers anyone can pull regardless of seniority.
points: Surveying over 6,000 knowledge workers, Friedman found the traits people assume drive team reputation (caring, good listener, funny) ranked lowest; the traits that actually mattered all directly improved team performance.
On Superteams, sharing credit -- actively naming who else contributed to a win -- was a stronger predictor of being seen as both likable and competent than protecting credit for oneself.
Status equality, not hierarchy, distinguished high-performing teams: members who feel equal in influence speak up and challenge ideas more, while status gaps push people toward self-protection.

The most revealing single question in the research was what people said they'd do with unexpected free time at work -- Superteam members defaulted to helping a colleague rather than protecting their own time.
quotes: The people who get the best opportunities are not always the smartest or most technically skilled. They're the people others trust. The people colleagues want on important projects.

The least-selected traits were: Caring. Good listener. Funny. That doesn't mean those qualities are unimportant. But they don't necessarily move you or your team any closer to accomplishing tasks or achieving goals.

On Superteams, teammates were significantly more likely to share credit for accomplishments by acknowledging or thanking others who contributed to their success. Research shows that people who share credit tend to come across as both more likable and more competent.
Members of Superteams were far more likely to feel equal in influence with their teammates. On average teams, people were more likely to feel either above or below one another.

On Superteams, workers were far more likely to say they would use the time helping someone else. What teammates choose to do when nobody's watching says more about the health of a team than almost any engagement survey.
When people feel lower in status, they become less likely to speak up, challenge ideas, or share concerns. They protect themselves instead of contributing fully.
